title: A Fun Way To Teach Students How Not To Behave https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2018/09/08/a-fun-way-to-teach-students-how-not-to-behave/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes a technique for teaching students not to repeat a misbehavior by mirroring it back to them later, waiting until the next day or a couple hours afterward rather than reacting in the moment. Because students recognize themselves in the modeling, it strikes at their pride and makes the behavior feel awkward or embarrassing, especially when delivered with exaggeration and humor rather than lecture. The article's central refinement is attributing the misbehavior to an imaginary student, such as 'Bobo' or 'Lulu,' which keeps the exercise lighthearted, avoids singling out real students, and lets teachers exaggerate the behavior for comic effect. He notes even high school students enjoy this approach when they trust the teacher, and that students often ask playful follow-up questions about the imaginary characters. Underneath the humor, he stresses, there remains a serious undercurrent of accountability tied to the classroom management plan.
points: The strategy involves modeling a repeated student misbehavior back to the class later—waiting until the next day or a few hours afterward, not in the moment.
Seeing themselves reflected in the modeling strikes students' pride, making the behavior feel awkward or embarrassing, especially when delivered with humor.
Attributing the behavior to an imaginary student (e.g., 'Bobo' or 'Lulu') keeps the exercise lighthearted and avoids singling out real students.
Using imaginary characters allows the teacher to exaggerate the behavior for comic effect without personal targeting.
Even high school students respond well to this approach when they trust the teacher, and it must be paired with genuine follow-through on the classroom management plan.
quotes: One of the most effective classroom management strategies is teaching students how not to behave .
It’s an effective strategy because when students see themselves in your modeling, they become less likely to repeat the behavior. The reason is that it strikes a nerve atop their personal pride.
One of the keys to making the strategy work is to have fun with it. It’s your exaggeration and humor that cause students to rethink taking part in the behavior again.
The solution is to personify the behavior in an imaginary student. When it’s attributed to someone who doesn’t exist—Bobo or Lulu, for example—then it naturally adds a lightheartedness to the lesson.
It’s fun. But more than anything, it makes the how-not strategy more effective. It keeps the tone upbeat and less personal—as you’ll never single out a specific student.
Your students will know that beneath the humor . . . Beats the heart of a leader that accepts nothing less than their very best.
